title: @classmethod, @staticmethod, and Dataclasses
relevance: Interviewers probe whether candidates know when to use class/static methods and can cut boilerplate with dataclasses instead of hand-rolling __init__/__repr__/__eq__.

phases.goal: Establish what instance, class, and static methods are, and what a dataclass automatically provides.

must_hit.point: An instance method takes self as its first parameter and can modify the specific object it was called on.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts instance methods with self vs alternatives that do not bind to one instance.

must_hit.point: A class method takes the class itself as its first parameter (by convention cls) and can read/modify class-level state but not instance-level state.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names cls and says it operates on the class, not a single instance.

must_hit.point: A static method takes neither self nor cls as an implicit first argument; it behaves like a normal function living in the class namespace.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says no implicit self/cls and treats it as a namespaced utility.

must_hit.point: A dataclass (@dataclass) automatically generates boilerplate such as __init__, __repr__, and __eq__.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate lists generated methods and mentions the @dataclass decorator.

must_hit.point: Python 3.7 introduced dataclasses for classes that primarily store data.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate cites Python 3.7 as when dataclasses arrived for data-holding classes.

probes: What is the difference between an instance method, a @classmethod, and a @staticmethod?
What does @dataclass generate for you that you would otherwise write by hand?

hints.1: Think about what each method type receives as its first argument—or whether it receives one at all.
hints.2: Instance → self; classmethod → cls and class state; staticmethod → neither; dataclass → auto __init__/__repr__/__eq__.
hints.3: Say: instance methods bind to an object via self; @classmethod gets cls for class-level work; @staticmethod is a plain function in the class; @dataclass auto-builds __init__, __repr__, and __eq__.

phases.goal: Show how classmethods act as alternative constructors with cls, and how dataclasses use type hints and optional post-init setup.

must_hit.point: @classmethod binds the method to the class and passes the class (cls) as the implicit first argument.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes the decorator binding and the implicit cls argument.

must_hit.point: Alternative constructors often use @classmethod and return cls(...) so subclasses get subclass instances instead of a hardcoded parent type.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains from_string-style constructors and why cls() beats hardcoding Date().

must_hit.point: Dataclasses require type hints (e.g. : str) even though Python does not strictly enforce them at runtime.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate notes annotated fields on the class body and that hints are not runtime-enforced.

must_hit.point: Custom setup right after dataclass construction is done via __post_init__ (e.g. derived fields).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names __post_init__ for logic that should run after the generated __init__.

probes: Why use cls() inside a classmethod constructor instead of hardcoding the class name?
If a dataclass generates __init__, how do you run custom setup right after creation?

hints.1: Subclassing and 'what happens after fields are set' are the two mechanics to nail.
hints.2: Alternative constructors return cls(...); post-construction dataclass logic goes in __post_init__.
hints.3: Say: cls() preserves subclass type for alternative constructors; use __post_init__ for derived fields after dataclass __init__.

phases.goal: Decide when class/static methods and dataclasses help versus when a plain function or hand-written class is better.

must_hit.point: Prefer a module-level function over @staticmethod when the function does not need the class—do not force functions into classes just to mimic Java.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says staticmethod is optional namespacing and module-level is often preferred.

must_hit.point: Use @staticmethod for utilities that need no class/instance data but conceptually belong with the class.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate gives a belonging-with-the-class rationale without claiming access to self/cls.

must_hit.point: Dataclasses fit data-heavy models; they are inappropriate when the class is primarily logic-heavy or needs complex validation during initialization.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts data containers with logic-heavy or heavily validated types.

probes: When would you put a utility on the class with @staticmethod versus defining it at module level?
When is a dataclass a bad fit compared to a normal class?

hints.1: Ask whether the function needs the class at all, and whether the type is mostly data or mostly behavior/validation.
hints.2: No class coupling → module function; conceptual grouping only → staticmethod; data-heavy → dataclass; logic-heavy/complex init validation → plain class.
hints.3: Say: avoid overusing @staticmethod—module-level is fine; dataclasses shine for data models and break down for logic-heavy classes or complex init validation.

phases.goal: Apply alternative constructors and dataclass field declarations to concrete examples.

must_hit.point: An alternative constructor like Date.from_string can parse a date string and return a new instance via cls(year, month, day).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate sketches parsing and returning cls(...) from a classmethod.

must_hit.point: A Product dataclass is declared with @dataclass and typed fields such as name: str and price (with a type annotation).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate writes @dataclass class Product with annotated name and price fields.

must_hit.point: Calling a static utility via the class (e.g. MathUtils.add) works without constructing an instance.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate invokes the static method on the class name with no instance.

probes: Write a @classmethod alternative constructor that builds an instance from a string.
Sketch a Product dataclass with name and price fields.

hints.1: Reuse the Date.from_string and Product dataclass patterns from the material.
hints.2: Classmethod: parse, then return cls(...). Dataclass: from dataclasses import dataclass, annotate fields.
hints.3: Say: @classmethod def from_string(cls, s): parse and return cls(...); @dataclass class Product: name: str; price: <annotated type>.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: @staticmethod is fine when a utility conceptually belongs on the class but needs neither self nor cls; if it does not need the class at all, a standalone module-level function is acceptable and often preferred—do not nest functions in classes just to mimic Java.

Dataclasses cut boilerplate (__init__, __repr__, __eq__) for data-heavy models with type-hinted fields; prefer a normal class when the type is primarily logic-heavy or needs complex validation during initialization.

tradeoffs.topic: @classmethod vs hardcoding the class in a factory
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Alternative constructors should call cls(...) so subclasses get subclass instances; hardcoding the parent class name (e.g. Date(...)) breaks that inheritance-friendly pattern.

gotchas.trap: Overusing @staticmethod and stuffing unrelated utilities into a class to look like Java.
gotchas.correction: If the function does not need the class, define it at module level; use @staticmethod only when namespacing with the class is genuinely useful.

gotchas.trap: Hardcoding the class name inside an alternative constructor (e.g. return Date(...)).
gotchas.correction: Return cls(...) so subclassing still constructs the subclass, not always the parent.

gotchas.trap: Reaching for a dataclass on a logic-heavy type or one that needs complex init-time validation.
gotchas.correction: Dataclasses suit data-heavy models; use a normal class when behavior or complex validation dominates initialization.

gotchas.trap: Assuming dataclass type hints are enforced at runtime.
gotchas.correction: Dataclasses require type hints in the declaration, but Python does not strictly enforce them at runtime.
